item.title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
item.description:
Skim new method — Ab initio construction of order n=8 Trotter-Suzuki product formulas, yielding more efficient compositions and the first generic schemes (q≥27 cycles). With ZNE mitigation at two-qubit depolarizing rate p2q=10−5, the n=8 scheme reaches minimal infidelity 0.0034% versus 0.034% for second-order Leapfrog.

Grade 0.494 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms and Quantum Error Mitigation”

Figure

Experimental error Errnexp. versus computational cost q/h for global and local operator groupings on an L=6 Heisenberg XZ chain. The author's recommended q=21 composition and q=30 generic schemes consistently outperform the baseline schemes by Morales et al.

Asks

Can Omelyan's direct error-term optimization approach be extended to order n=8 to derive more efficient Trotter decompositions than existing compositions of second-order schemes?

Before

Morales et al. composition schemes at order n=8.

But

Simulated quantum circuits; evaluated on 1D open-boundary Heisenberg XZ spin chains (L=6); depolarizing noise model.

Tools

Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion · free Lie algebra commutator basis · pybch · constrained numerical optimization · qiskit-omelyan

Abstract

Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order n could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond 6^th order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to 6^th order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order n = 8, and find both more efficient compositions and the first 8^th order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

item.title: Mitigating large circuits with a learned small-circuit mitigator
item.description:
Skim new method — GNN trained on 4-qubit circuits up to depth 15 mitigates circuits up to 28 qubits and depth 103 via circuit cutting. Recovers 88% to 98% of noise-induced energy error on a 24-site holographic Ising chain.

Grade 0.516 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fundamental limits of quantum error mitigation”

Figure

Energy per site E/(NJ) versus transverse field strength h/J for a 24-site holographic Ising chain at a fixed budget of 2×105 shots per basis. The pretrained GNN mitigator reconstructs energies closer to the exact ground state than CDR or PEC across all fields evaluated.

Asks

Can an error-mitigation neural network trained solely on small circuits be reused via circuit cutting to infer noise-free observables of much larger and deeper circuits without retraining?

Before

Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation applied to the same cut fragments; GNN out-recovers energy error against both under fixed shot budgets.

But

Depolarizing and amplitude-damping simulation (plus hardware calibration test); sampling overhead grows exponentially with the cut count; requires circuits partitionable into 4-qubit, depth-15 fragments.

Tools

gate and wire circuit cutting · graph isomorphism network (GINE) · classical tensor contraction

Abstract

Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.
